stories.title: Singapore Says Goodbye to a China Leader Who Changed the World
stories.headline_kid: Zhu Rongji, a former top leader of China, has passed away at 97, and Singapore's Prime Minister sent kind words to China.
summary: Zhu Rongji was China's premier from 1998 to 2003. A premier is like the country's chief manager — he runs the government's daily work, while the president is more like the head figure. Zhu passed away on Wednesday due to illness, at the grand age of 97.

Zhu is remembered for helping China join the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2002. Think of the WTO like a giant trading club — countries in it agree to follow fair rules when buying and selling goods with each other. Joining this club helped China's economy grow hugely over the following years.

Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong sent his condolences — a message of sympathy and respect — to China's current premier, Li Qiang. This shows how closely Singapore and China work together, even during sad moments.

Zhu even visited Singapore before, back in 2000, for a regional meeting. His passing is a reminder of how leaders from other countries can shape trade and daily life far beyond their own borders — including the products we use here in Singapore.

lenses.me: Some toys, gadgets or clothes you own might be cheaper today because of trade rules Zhu Rongji helped set up years ago.
lenses.family: Your parents might remember hearing about Zhu Rongji's reforms on the news when they were younger.
lenses.friends: It's a chance to talk about how one country's leader can affect trade and prices all over Asia, including Singapore.
lenses.nation: Singapore's condolence message shows how important good relations with China are for our trade and diplomacy.
lenses.world: China joining the WTO under Zhu's leadership helped turn it into one of the world's biggest economies, changing global trade forever.

stories.title: Japan Gets Its Worst-Ever Rain Warning
stories.headline_kid: Non-stop heavy rain flooded homes and roads in Japan, so serious that 100,000 households were told to leave for safety.
summary: Torrential rain — meaning extremely heavy, non-stop rain — poured over eastern Japan on Thursday. It caused landslides (when soil and rocks suddenly slide down a slope) and cut off electricity in many homes.

Japan's weather agency issued its highest-level heavy rain warning for the area for the very first time. Think of it like the loudest possible alarm bell — it means the danger is extremely serious and people must act fast.
More than 100,000 households were urged to evacuate, which means leave their homes to somewhere safer. News videos showed cars stuck and submerged in floodwater near Chiba, a city close to Tokyo.

This matters to Singaporean families too — Japan is a very popular holiday destination for us. If your family is planning a trip there, it's wise to check weather updates, as flights and trains could be delayed by storms like this.

lenses.me: If you're dreaming of a Japan trip, remember weather can change holiday plans suddenly.
lenses.family: Families with upcoming Japan holidays should watch the news for updates before flying.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with classmates how climate change seems to be making storms more extreme worldwide.
lenses.nation: Singapore also faces extreme weather like heavy haze and heatwaves — a reminder that we all need to prepare for climate surprises.
lenses.world: Scientists say climate change is making heavy rain events like this happen more often and more severely across the world.

stories.title: Rescued From Kidnappers... But Also Wanted By Police
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean man was saved from kidnappers in Malaysia, but now police want to question him too — because he might know the kidnapper himself.
summary: A 32-year-old Singaporean man and a 33-year-old Singaporean woman were rescued by Malaysian police after being kidnapped. This is the latest in a string of kidnapping rescues involving Singaporeans in Malaysia this past week.

But there's a surprising twist: Singapore's Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) — the agency that deals with illegal drugs — wants to speak to the rescued man. Police say he had no valid travel document, meaning he wasn't allowed to properly enter or leave the country.

More strangely, investigators believe he might actually know one of the alleged kidnappers. This makes his case more complicated than a simple rescue — he could be a witness, or even involved somehow.

This story is a good reminder to always be careful about who you trust, especially with money matters or unofficial travel arrangements, and why following rules (like having proper documents) matters for staying safe.

lenses.me: It reminds you to never keep secrets from trusted adults if something feels unsafe or suspicious.
lenses.family: Parents may feel more cautious about family members travelling without proper documents.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with friends why it's risky to get involved in shady deals, even if you know someone.
lenses.nation: Singapore and Malaysia's police continue working together to solve kidnapping cases and keep citizens safe.
lenses.world: Cross-border crimes like this show why countries must cooperate closely to catch criminals who cross borders.

stories.title: Malaysia Tightens Hiking Rules After Too Many Rescues
stories.headline_kid: More hikers in Malaysia are getting stuck or hurt while chasing perfect photos for social media, so new safety rules are coming.
summary: Malaysia is introducing stricter hiking rules after a jump in search-and-rescue cases, where mountain rescue teams have to go find lost or injured hikers. Experts say social media is partly to blame.

Many hikers now chase 'aesthetic' — meaning beautiful, picture-perfect — photos for platforms like Instagram or TikTok. In doing so, some underestimate (don't take seriously enough) the real dangers of mountaineering, like sudden weather changes or steep, slippery paths.

This matters for Singaporeans too, since many families and students love hiking trips to places like Mount Kinabalu in Malaysia during the school holidays. The new rules might mean needing permits, guides, or more safety checks before setting off.
The bigger lesson here: no photo is worth risking your safety. Adventures are best enjoyed when you respect nature and follow safety guidelines, not just chase 'likes' online.

lenses.me: If you go hiking, remember that following safety rules matters more than getting a cool photo.
lenses.family: Families planning hiking holidays to Malaysia may need to check new permit or guide requirements.
lenses.friends: You could talk with friends about whether social media pressure makes people take unsafe risks.
lenses.nation: Since many Singaporeans hike in Malaysia, these new rules could affect upcoming school trips or family holidays.
lenses.world: This story shows a global pattern — social media trends sometimes push people to take real-world risks for online attention.

stories.title: Some Campus Tours at NUS and NTU Are Secretly Unofficial!
stories.headline_kid: A university student is secretly running paid tours of NUS and NTU on a travel app — and earning more money than official student guides!
summary: NUS (National University of Singapore) and NTU (Nanyang Technological University) are two of Singapore's top universities — like the big schools students dream of attending after junior college or polytechnic. Their beautiful campuses attract many visitors.

It turns out some students are running unauthorised (not officially approved) campus tours, listed on a third-party travel booking platform — similar to how you might book a holiday activity online. These tours are not organised by the universities themselves.
One student running these tours says he earns about S$40 an hour — more than what official student ambassadors, who are trained and approved by the university, usually make.

This raises interesting questions: Is it fair for unofficial guides to earn more? Could visitors get wrong information about the campus? It shows how popular Singapore's top universities have become, even among tourists and prospective students.

lenses.me: If you ever visit a university campus, you'll now know to check if your tour guide is official!
lenses.family: Parents thinking of joining a campus tour for an older sibling should check if it's authorised first.
lenses.friends: It's an interesting topic to discuss — would you take an unofficial tour if it seemed fun, even if it wasn't approved?
lenses.nation: This shows how much interest there is in Singapore's universities, boosting our reputation for good education.
lenses.world: Online platforms connecting people globally raise new questions about who checks the quality and safety of such services.
